objectives.text: Explain what automation is, with everyday examples (ATM, washing machine, bank SMS, supermarket stock, thank-you emails, scheduled newsletters), and what automation is not (it does not think, learn or understand; it follows rules people create).

quiz.question: What is automation?
options: Teaching a computer to think about each task and choose the best way to do it
Making a computer or machine do a task by itself, following set instructions the same way every time
Replacing every worker in a business with robots
Writing complex computer code that only big tech companies can afford
quiz.explanation: Automation means making a computer or machine perform a task automatically, following instructions exactly the same way every single time.

quiz.question: In the automated morning-report example, what happens at 8:00 AM?
options: The computer performs the first step and waits for a person to do the rest
A staff member is reminded to start the six steps by hand
The computer decides which of the six steps are needed that day
The computer performs all six steps instantly, with no human touching it
quiz.explanation: In the example, the manual routine of opening Excel, downloading, copying, pasting, saving and emailing is done by the computer at 8:00 AM without any human.

quiz.question: A customer buys bread at a supermarket and the stock count drops by one with nobody updating it. Which best describes what happened?
options: The system followed a rule that lowers stock after each sale
A staff member updated the count after the sale
The system decided the shop needed less bread
The system learned the customer's buying habits
quiz.explanation: When bread is purchased, inventory reduces by one automatically, so no manual stock updates are required.

quiz.question: A visitor fills in a form on a website and instantly gets a 'Thank you' email. Who typed that email?
options: The website owner, who writes it quickly after each form
A customer-care officer who watches the form all day
Nobody; the system sends it automatically
The visitor, who writes the message to themselves
quiz.explanation: In website automation, a form submission leads to an instant 'Thank you' email and no one types those messages manually.

quiz.question: In the door analogy, 'Whenever someone rings the bell, open the door.' What does the system do when the bell rings?
options: It checks who is at the door and opens only for people it trusts
It opens the door without judging who is there
It waits for someone to decide whether to open
It learns from past visitors and then decides
quiz.explanation: The system does not judge who is at the door; it simply executes the command it was given.

quiz.question: Which statement about how an automated machine works is correct?
options: It thinks about each task before acting on it
It makes its own choices when rules are unclear
It keeps its own rules and ignores those given
It does not think; it only follows the rules it is given
quiz.explanation: The rules of the machine: it does not think, it does not make decisions, and it follows the rules you provide.

quiz.question: A computer has the rule 'If salary is above ₦300,000, approve loan. Else, reject loan.' Why does it approve or reject a person?
options: It follows the rule, but it does not know why the rule exists
It understands each person's situation and chooses fairly
It learns from earlier loans and adjusts the limit
It guesses what the bank manager would prefer
quiz.explanation: Automation is not intelligence. The computer is not thinking, learning or understanding; it simply follows the rule.

quiz.question: The bank changes the loan rule so that the salary limit is higher. What must happen to the automation?
options: Nothing; the computer will figure out the new limit by itself
The computer will slowly learn the new limit from applicants
A person must change the automation to use the new rule
The old rule will update itself at the end of the month
quiz.explanation: If tomorrow the rule changes, you must change the automation. The computer cannot figure it out.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of automation?
options: It follows rules
It improves itself over time
It repeats tasks
It needs humans to create the rules
quiz.explanation: Automation follows rules, repeats tasks, does not think, does not learn, does not improve itself and needs humans to create the rules.

quiz.question: You enter your PIN and ask the ATM for ₦20,000, but you actually needed ₦30,000. Why does the ATM only give ₦20,000?
options: It decided ₦20,000 was enough for you
It learned from your past withdrawals
It was waiting for a staff member to approve more
It follows the steps and does not ask itself whether you might need more
quiz.explanation: The ATM follows steps. It does not ask itself, 'Maybe this customer needs ₦30,000.' It follows the instructions.

quiz.question: You select Cotton and 30 minutes on a washing machine, and the clothes are very dirty. What does the machine do?
options: It runs the selected program anyway
It senses the dirt and washes for longer
It stops and asks you to choose again
It switches to a stronger setting by itself
quiz.explanation: The washing machine does not decide. It simply follows the selected program.

quiz.question: Every Monday at 8 AM, customers receive a newsletter and nobody presses Send. Who or what sends it?
options: A staff member who presses Send from home
The customers, who request it each Monday
The software, on its set schedule
An AI that decides each week whether to send
quiz.explanation: In email automation, the software sends the newsletter automatically at the set time.

quiz.question: Your bank sends you an SMS the moment money enters your account. Why is this an example of automation?
options: A bank worker reads each transaction and writes a message
Software sends the message the same way every time, with nobody typing it
The bank decides each time whether you deserve an alert
The message is only sent when you call the bank
quiz.explanation: Nobody at the bank types the SMS; software does it automatically, the same way, every single time.

quiz.question: You are not sure whether something counts as automation. Which question from the lessons helps you check?
options: Does this need a computer with the latest software?
Would a human enjoy doing this task?
Does this task involve sending an email?
If this happened 100 times, would the steps ever change?
quiz.explanation: If the answer to 'would the steps ever change in 100 repeats?' is no, that is a strong sign of automation.

quiz.question: What does automation remove from work?
options: The boring, repeated parts of a task
The need for people in every task
All tasks that involve a customer
The need to ever write any rules
quiz.explanation: A common mistake is thinking automation replaces humans completely. It removes the repeated parts but not the need for people.

quiz.question: According to the summary, what is automation mainly about?
options: Intelligence and creativity, so computers can replace humans
Learning from data, so tasks improve over time
Efficiency and consistency, so humans can focus on other work
Making work look modern, so customers are impressed
quiz.explanation: By setting clear rules we let systems handle repetitive tasks, so humans can focus on other work.

quiz.question: What shift does a motion-sensor light show compared with an ordinary light switch?
options: From a light that is on all day to one that is off
From a human noticing and acting to software noticing and acting
From a simple tool to one that thinks about the room
From a device that costs money to one that is free
quiz.explanation: A switch needs a person to notice darkness and flip it; a motion sensor notices and switches on by itself. That is the shift automation makes.

quiz.question: Which of these is something you may already use without realising it is automation?
options: Counting change by hand at a shop counter
A tailor taking measurements with a tape
Writing a customer's order in a notebook
A phone backing up your photos to the cloud every night
quiz.explanation: Phone photo backups, birthday reminders and auto-correct are everyday automation working in the background.

quiz.question: A colleague says, 'Our automation will learn what customers like and get smarter on its own.' What is the best reply?
options: Automation does not learn; people must change the rules
That is right, because automation learns from each task
That is right, but only after a month of use
That is wrong, because automation cannot follow rules
quiz.explanation: Automation does not learn and does not improve itself. Humans must create and change the rules.

quiz.question: Which of these is an automated step rather than a human one?
options: A cashier deciding whether to give a discount
A shopkeeper choosing what stock to buy next
A POS machine printing a receipt after payment
A manager calming an unhappy customer
quiz.explanation: A POS machine printing a receipt after payment follows the same steps every time, so software handles it without a person.

objectives.text: Tell manual workflows from automated workflows, and judge whether a task is a strong or weak automation candidate (frequent, predictable, the same steps every time, not needing human judgment such as empathy, negotiation or a unique decision).

quiz.question: What is a manual workflow?
options: A task that is always slow because it uses paper instead of phones.
A task where a human has to do every single step, every single time.
A task where software does most steps and a person only checks the result.
A task that is done only once a year by the business owner.
quiz.explanation: In a manual workflow a person does every step each time. Software is not doing the repetitive parts.

quiz.question: What is an automated workflow?
options: Software does everything, and no person is ever involved at any point.
A person writes every step down in a notebook before doing it.
Software handles the repeated steps, and a person steps in only when needed.
A person does each step faster by using a phone or computer.
quiz.explanation: Automated workflows still involve people for judgment calls. Software takes the repeated steps.

quiz.question: Which set describes a strong automation candidate?
options: It happens daily, but each case needs the owner's fresh decision.
It happens often, follows the same steps, and a slight delay is no problem.
It is important to the business and must be done at the exact second.
It is simple to explain, but it happens only once or twice a year.
quiz.explanation: A strong candidate is frequent, follows the same steps every time, and is not time-critical to the second.

quiz.question: Which question helps you decide whether a step is a sign of automation?
options: Would my customers notice if I stopped doing it?
Is this task difficult to learn?
If this happened 100 times, would the steps ever change?
Does this task use a computer already?
quiz.explanation: If the steps would never change across 100 repeats, that is a strong sign the task can be automated.

quiz.question: A POS machine prints a receipt the moment a payment is confirmed. What is this an example of?
options: An automated workflow
A weak automation candidate
A manual workflow
A task needing human judgment
quiz.explanation: The software handles the repeated step with no person typing or printing by hand.

Personally welcoming a new member.
quiz.explanation: Recording names and numbers is repetitive and predictable. Welcoming and counselling need a real human.

quiz.question: Which belief is a common mistake about automation?
options: That automation can remove boring repeated parts of work.
That automation lets people spend time on judgment work.
That automation fits tasks that follow the same steps.
That automation means replacing humans completely.
quiz.explanation: Automation removes the repeated parts, not the need for people.

quiz.question: A beginner says every workflow must be either fully manual or fully automated. What is true in real life?
options: Mixed workflows cannot work because software cannot sit beside people.
Most good automations are a mix of software for repeated steps and people for judgment.
Most workflows are fully manual and are best left that way.
Most good automations have no person involved once they are set up.
quiz.explanation: Good automations usually share the work: software for repetition, humans for judgment.

quiz.question: Which task is the weakest candidate for automation?
options: Resolving an angry customer's complaint.
Sending a thank-you message to every online buyer.
Replying with the same shop opening hours to new customers.
Sending the same order confirmation to every customer.
quiz.explanation: A complaint needs empathy and a unique decision, so it is poor for automation. The others are the same every time.

quiz.question: A bank sends you an SMS the moment money enters or leaves your account. Why is this a good example of automation?
options: The message is different for every customer after careful thought.
The SMS is sent only when the customer asks for it.
Nobody types the message; software sends it the same way every single time.
A bank staff member types each message very quickly.
quiz.explanation: The SMS is repetitive and identical in steps, so software does it without a person.

quiz.question: In the Manual vs Automated chart, what does a tick next to a step mean?
options: The step needs the most human care.
The step is repetitive and predictable.
The step has already been finished.
The step is not important to the business.
quiz.explanation: A tick means the step never changes. It does not mean the step is unimportant.

quiz.question: What does 'Frequent is not the same as automatable' warn you about?
options: Any step that happens often can be left to software.
Only steps done once a day can be automated.
Rare steps are always better to automate.
A step can happen often and still need a human touch.
quiz.explanation: Frequency alone is not enough. Steps involving deciding, negotiating or comforting need a human.

quiz.question: In the chart exercise, what do the circled steps show?
options: Steps that still need a human, such as those needing judgment or empathy.
Steps that were forgotten when the list was first written.
Steps that software can do faster than a person could.

quiz.explanation: Circled steps are the unticked ones, the true human-only moments in the task.

quiz.question: Why does the lesson say to start with the smallest, most repetitive task you can find?
options: Bigger tasks never contain any repeated steps worth automating.
Small tasks never need any human checking once automated.
Small wins build your confidence before you tackle anything bigger.
Beginners are not allowed to automate anything larger.
quiz.explanation: Starting small gives quick wins and builds confidence before bigger tasks.

quiz.question: Typing customer orders from WhatsApp into a notebook by hand is an example of what?

An automation opportunity already solved
An automated workflow
A manual workflow
quiz.explanation: A human does every step each time, so this is a manual workflow.

quiz.question: Which everyday thing is automation quietly working in the background?
options: Counting change by hand at a market stall
A friend phoning to remind you of a birthday
Your phone auto-correcting your spelling
Writing a shopping list on paper
quiz.explanation: Auto-correct and app birthday reminders run without you doing the repeated step by hand.

quiz.question: Which quality is part of a great automation candidate, according to the Pro Tip?
options: It must be done at the exact second.
Getting it slightly delayed would not cause a disaster.
It is done only by senior staff.
It changes its steps depending on the customer.
quiz.explanation: A good candidate happens often, follows the same steps and is not time-critical to the second.

quiz.question: Which is an example of a repetitive task?
options: Replying 'Good afternoon, our shop opens by 8am' to every new customer message.
Choosing a new shop location.
Writing a unique wedding speech.
Negotiating a price with a supplier.
quiz.explanation: A repetitive task is something done the exact same way again and again.

quiz.question: Before you can automate anything, which skill does the lesson say comes first?
options: Noticing the repetitive things you do over and over again
Choosing the most advanced software on the market
Writing computer code for each of your tasks
Hiring someone to take over your repeated tasks
quiz.explanation: You cannot automate something you have not first learned to spot, so noticing repetition comes first.

quiz.question: In the light switch and motion sensor idea, what shift does automation make?
options: From one person doing the work to two people doing it.
From a light that is off to a light that is on.
From a human noticing and acting to software noticing and acting.
From a cheap tool to an expensive tool.
quiz.explanation: A switch needs a person to notice the dark. A motion sensor notices and acts by itself.

objectives.text: Explain what AI is and how AI automation differs from rule-based automation (rules vs understanding/predicting/deciding; examples: email sorting, customer support, CV screening, fraud detection, medical triage), including its limits and the continuing need for humans to build, monitor and review it.

quiz.question: What is Artificial Intelligence (AI) trying to do?
options: Make computers perform tasks that normally require human intelligence
Make a computer repeat the same steps without any change
Replace every worker in a business
Store large amounts of data in spreadsheets
quiz.explanation: AI tries to make computers do tasks that normally need human intelligence. Repeating fixed steps is ordinary automation.

quiz.question: Which list shows things AI can do that a plain rule cannot?
options: Follow fixed rules, repeat tasks, never think and never learn
Open Excel, copy data, paste it and save it
Recognize patterns, understand language, identify pictures and predict outcomes
Ring a bell, open a door and close it
quiz.explanation: AI can recognize patterns, understand language, identify pictures, predict outcomes, generate content and make recommendations. The other lists describe ordinary automation.

quiz.question: What is AI Automation?
options: Using automation to send scheduled emails and messages without any person involved
Using AI together with automation so the system can make intelligent decisions before acting
Using a robot that handles every business task without human help
Using faster computers to follow the same written rules each time
quiz.explanation: AI Automation combines AI (the decision part) with automation (the action part).

quiz.question: A rule says: if an email contains the word 'Invoice', move it to the Finance folder. What happens to an email about a payment that never uses the word 'Invoice'?
options: The rule understands it is about payment and moves it anyway
The computer learns the new wording and updates its own rule
The computer asks the sender what the email means
The rule does not catch it, because the rule only looks for that word
quiz.explanation: Rule-based automation only does what its rule says. AI can understand that an email is about payment even when the word never appears.

quiz.question: A loan rule says: if salary is above ₦300,000, approve; else reject. The bank changes its policy. What must happen?
options: The computer will notice the policy change and adjust itself
The computer will keep the old rule but explain why it is wrong
A person must change the automation, because the computer cannot figure it out
Nothing, because automation improves itself over time
quiz.explanation: Automation does not think, learn or improve itself. If the rule changes, humans must change the automation.

quiz.question: Why does a rule-based loan automation reject someone earning ₦290,000?
options: It has studied the person's spending and decided they are risky
It simply follows the rule and does not know why the rule exists
It understood the person's situation and judged them
It predicted the person would not repay
quiz.explanation: The computer is not thinking or understanding. It only follows the instruction it was given.

quiz.question: A bank rule blocks an account only if a withdrawal is above ₦5 million. A thief withdraws ₦20,000. How could AI Automation help?
options: It can spot unusual location, device or time and predict fraud
It can lower the ₦5 million limit by itself after a theft
It can wait until withdrawals add up beyond ₦5 million
It can ask the owner to retype the PIN every time
quiz.explanation: AI looks at patterns such as unusual location, spending, device and time, so it can predict fraud even when the amount is small.

quiz.question: A rule shortlists a CV only if the applicant has more than 5 years of experience. How does an AI-based approach differ?
options: It counts the years of experience and shortlists anyone above a number
It looks for one keyword in the CV and files matching CVs together
It picks the first CVs received and leaves the rest for staff
It reads the whole CV and ranks candidates by what it understands
quiz.explanation: AI does not depend on a fixed rule like '5 years only'. It reads the whole CV and ranks the candidates.

quiz.question: A simple medical rule flags a patient if temperature is above 38°C. What does AI Automation examine instead of temperature alone?
options: Only the temperature, but checked more often
Symptoms, X-rays, blood tests and medical history
The patient's age and the time of arrival
A fixed list of diseases matched to one number
quiz.explanation: AI examines many kinds of information and predicts possible diseases, while the rule looks at one number.

objectives.text: Describe the three building blocks of automation (trigger, action, workflow) and identify them in real scenarios (what starts it, what it does next, the complete sequence).

quiz.question: Every automation is made up of which three simple parts?
options: Trigger, report and schedule
Trigger, action and workflow
Input, storage and output
Form, spreadsheet and email
quiz.explanation: Every automation is built from a trigger (what starts it), actions (the tasks done) and a workflow (the complete sequence).

quiz.question: What is a trigger in automation?
options: The event that starts an automation
The task performed after something happens
The full list of steps from start to finish
The tool used to build the automation
quiz.explanation: A trigger is the event that starts an automation. The task that follows is an action, and the full sequence is the workflow.

quiz.question: What is an action in automation?
options: The event that begins the automation
The complete sequence of steps together
A person who checks every message by hand
A task performed after the trigger occurs
quiz.explanation: The trigger starts the automation and the action performs the work.

quiz.question: What is a workflow?
options: The single event that starts an automation
One single task done after the trigger occurs
The full sequence of triggers and actions
A platform for building without writing code
quiz.explanation: A workflow joins the trigger and its actions into one complete process, like a recipe with several steps.

quiz.question: What happens in an automation before its trigger occurs?
options: The first action runs and then waits
Nothing happens until the trigger occurs
All the actions run once as a test
The workflow sends a reminder to the owner
quiz.explanation: An automation stays idle. The trigger is like the Start button, and nothing begins until it is pressed.

quiz.question: Which everyday item is used to describe a workflow?
options: A recipe, which has several steps
A doorbell, which starts something
A Start button, which begins things
An alarm clock, which wakes you up
quiz.explanation: A workflow is like a recipe: it contains several steps. The doorbell and alarm are examples of triggers, and the Start button describes a trigger.

quiz.question: In an online class business, which of these is a trigger rather than an action?
options: Send a receipt
Unlock the course
Notify the instructor
Payment completed
quiz.explanation: Payment completed is an event that starts the automation. Sending a receipt, unlocking the course and notifying the instructor are actions that follow.

quiz.question: Which of these is an action rather than a trigger?
options: Appointment booked
New email received
Send a welcome email
File uploaded
quiz.explanation: Sending a welcome email is a task the system performs. The other three are events that can start an automation.

quiz.question: Your doorbell rings and you open the door. Which part is the trigger?
options: You opening the door
The doorbell ringing
The person standing outside
The door being unlocked
quiz.explanation: The ringing is the event that starts things. Opening the door is the response, like an action.

quiz.question: The lesson compares automation to a row of dominoes. What idea does this show?
options: One event causes another event, which causes another
Every step must be done by hand, one at a time
All steps happen at exactly the same moment
An automation can only have two steps
quiz.explanation: Like dominoes, each step in an automation sets off the next one once the first event happens.

quiz.question: How should you think of a trigger?
options: Like a recipe with many steps
Like the task that does the work
Like the final Done message
Like pressing the Start button
quiz.explanation: A trigger is the Start button: nothing happens until it occurs. The recipe describes a workflow.

quiz.question: A customer pays for a course. Which group lists only actions that can follow?
options: Customer pays, send receipt, unlock the course
Customer pays, unlock the course, notify instructor
Send receipt, unlock the course, notify the instructor
New email received, send receipt, notify instructor
quiz.explanation: The payment is the trigger, so it cannot be in a list of actions. Receipt, unlocking and notifying are the actions.

quiz.question: How many actions can an automation have?
options: Exactly one action only
One or more actions
Always exactly five actions

objectives.text: Recognise and avoid the six common beginner mistakes (trying to automate everything, not understanding the process first, forgetting to test, ignoring errors, building very large workflows too soon, forgetting security).

quiz.question: How many common beginner mistakes does the course list for people starting with automation?
options: Three
Six
Four
Ten
quiz.explanation: The course lists six common beginner mistakes, from trying to automate everything to forgetting security.

quiz.question: Which advice goes with the mistake of trying to automate everything?
options: Start with simple, repetitive tasks and leave the rest manual.
Start with the most complex tasks and simplify them later.
Start with tasks that need a new decision every time.
Start with tasks that happen only once a year.
quiz.explanation: Not every task needs automation. Beginners should begin with simple, repetitive tasks.

quiz.question: What does the course say about a process you cannot explain clearly?
options: The automation tool will work it out for you.
You can automate it, then fix it later.
It only needs a trigger to be automated.
If you cannot explain it clearly, you cannot automate it.
quiz.explanation: Mistake 2 is not understanding the process first. You must be able to explain the process before automating it.

quiz.question: What should you do before building an automation, to avoid not understanding the process first?
options: Buy a paid automation plan.
Ask the tool to guess the steps.
Write down each step of the process.
Build the full workflow, then list the steps.
quiz.explanation: The advice is to always write down each step before building an automation.

quiz.question: A beginner builds an automation and immediately assumes it works. Which mistake is this?
options: Ignoring errors
Forgetting to test
Building very large workflows too soon
Trying to automate everything
quiz.explanation: Forgetting to test means assuming an automation works without checking. The advice is to test it several times.

quiz.question: How often should you test a new automation?
options: Several times
Once, then never again
Only if a customer complains
Never, if it looks correct on screen
quiz.explanation: The course says to always test the automation several times.

quiz.question: Which of these is given as a reason an automation might fail?
options: The task is too repetitive.
The workflow has a trigger.
The tool is no-code.
The login expires.
quiz.explanation: Listed causes of failure: internet drops, login expires, required information missing, permissions change.

quiz.question: Which mistake is about not checking whether your automation completed successfully?
options: Forgetting to test
Not understanding the process first
Ignoring errors
Forgetting security
quiz.explanation: Mistake 4 is ignoring errors. Always check whether your automation completed successfully.

quiz.question: What is wrong with building a workflow with dozens of steps as your first project?
options: Large workflows run more slowly than small ones.
Beginners should start small and improve gradually.
Large workflows should be built first and trimmed later.
Dozens of steps are normal for a first project.
quiz.explanation: Mistake 5 is building very large workflows too soon. The advice is to start small, learn, and improve gradually.

quiz.question: Why does the course say security matters when you build automations?
options: Automation often handles important information that needs protecting.
Automation tools often delete information that is unprotected.
Automation usually works only with information that is public.
Automation sends every message to the tool's owner first.
quiz.explanation: The Mistake 6 slide says automation often handles important information, so passwords, customer information, financial records and personal data must be protected.

quiz.question: Which of these should you protect, to avoid the mistake of forgetting security?
options: Only the names of your apps
Only your workflow's title
Nothing, because automation is automatically safe
Passwords and customer information
quiz.explanation: Automation often handles important information such as passwords, customer information, financial records and personal data.

quiz.question: What is the rule about sensitive information when working with automation?
options: Share it freely with everyone on the team.
Post it in the class group for checking.
Never share it unnecessarily.
Save it in the trigger name so it is easy to find.
quiz.explanation: Mistake 6 advice: never share sensitive information unnecessarily.

quiz.question: Which is the best size for a first automation?
options: Ten triggers and twenty actions
One trigger and one or two actions
A workflow covering the whole business
Five triggers and no actions
quiz.explanation: A simple workflow with one trigger and one or two actions is enough to build confidence.

quiz.question: Which pair of mistakes both come from trying to do too much?
options: Trying to automate everything and building very large workflows too soon
Forgetting to test and ignoring errors
Forgetting security and ignoring errors
Not understanding the process and forgetting to test
quiz.explanation: Both Mistake 1 and Mistake 5 are about going too big too early; the fix is to start small and simple.

quiz.question: A friend says every single task in the shop should be automated. Which beginner mistake is this?
options: Forgetting to test
Ignoring errors
Building very large workflows too soon
Trying to automate everything
quiz.explanation: Not every task needs automation. The first mistake is trying to automate everything instead of starting with simple, repetitive tasks.

quiz.question: Which beginner mistake would a missing 'required information' problem most directly connect to?
options: Trying to automate everything
Building very large workflows too soon
Ignoring errors
Not understanding the process first
quiz.explanation: Missing required information is one reason automations fail, and ignoring errors means not checking for such failures.

quiz.question: Which statement best explains why testing matters before using an automation in a real business?
options: Testing makes the automation run faster.
Assuming it works may let mistakes reach real customers.
Testing is only needed for large workflows.
Testing removes the need for a trigger.
quiz.explanation: Many beginners assume an automation works. Testing several times catches problems before they affect real work.

quiz.question: Ngozi automates her shop orders but never looks at the run results. Her login expired a week ago. Which advice did she miss?
options: Always check whether your automation completed successfully.
Start with simple, repetitive tasks.
Write down each step before building.
Never share sensitive information unnecessarily.
quiz.explanation: Expired logins are a listed cause of failure, and checking whether the automation completed would have revealed it.

quiz.question: Which of these lists contains only beginner mistakes from the course?
options: Writing the process, testing, starting small
Choosing a trigger, adding actions, saving the workflow

options.text: Begin with the calming of upset clients, since it is the most important.
options.outcome: That step needs a human, so it is a weak starting point.

options.text: Start with simple, repetitive tasks such as sending the same booking confirmation.
options.outcome: Her salon begins with a task that follows the same steps every time, which builds confidence.

options.text: Wait until she can build a 30-step workflow.
options.outcome: Large workflows are a beginner mistake; starting small works better.

options.text: Write down each step of how an order is handled before building anything.
options.outcome: If you cannot explain the process clearly, you cannot automate it, so writing the steps comes first.

options.text: Ask the automation to figure out the process itself.
options.outcome: Automation does not think; it only follows steps you provide.

options.text: Copy another bakery's workflow without checking it.

options.text: Nothing, since one successful try proves it works.
options.outcome: One try can hide problems; always test several times.

options.text: Delete the sheet so errors cannot appear.

objectives.text: Explain the business value of automation (saves time including the time arithmetic, saves money, reduces human errors, works 24 hours, improves customer experience, increases productivity) and where businesses use it.

quiz.question: A task takes 10 minutes and is repeated 50 times every day. How much time does it use in one day?
options: 60 minutes
500 minutes
150 minutes
5,000 minutes
quiz.explanation: Multiply the minutes per task by the number of repeats: 10 x 50 = 500 minutes a day.

quiz.question: The 500 minutes a day spent on a 10-minute task done 50 times is how long in hours?
options: About 5 hours
Exactly 50 hours
Less than 1 hour
Over 8 hours
quiz.explanation: 500 minutes divided by 60 is more than 8 hours, which is a full working day spent on one repeated task.

quiz.question: If automation takes over that 500-minute daily task, what is left for a person to do?
options: A few minutes of monitoring
The whole task, done faster
Nothing, and no one ever checks it
Another 500 minutes of typing
quiz.explanation: Automation can reduce the task to a few minutes of monitoring. A person still checks that it is running well.

quiz.question: Which statement best explains how automation saves money?
options: It lets the business stop serving customers directly
It makes every employee work longer hours for free
Staff spend less time on repetitive work and can do more valuable work
It removes the need for any computer or software
quiz.explanation: Employees who are freed from repetitive work can serve customers, make sales, or solve complex problems, so the business gains more value from the same people.

quiz.question: A business wants to handle more work without hiring more people for repetitive admin tasks. Which benefit does this describe?
options: Works 24 hours
Improves customer experience
Saves money
Reduces human errors
quiz.explanation: Businesses can often accomplish more work without increasing staff for repetitive administrative tasks, which is how automation saves money.

quiz.question: Why does automation reduce human errors?
options: It performs the same steps consistently, while people get tired and forget
It thinks carefully about each step before acting
It learns from every mistake that staff make
It checks the work of staff after they finish it
quiz.explanation: People become tired, forget, and make mistakes. Automation repeats the same steps the same way each time. It does not think or judge.

quiz.question: Automation is described as working 24 hours. Which condition applies?
options: It only runs during normal office hours
It stops on weekends and public holidays
It needs a person to restart it every night
It keeps running as long as the required systems are available
quiz.explanation: Automation can run mornings, afternoons, nights, weekends and public holidays, provided the systems it needs are available.

quiz.question: Which of these is something customers get when a business uses automation well?
options: Slower but more personal replies
Faster responses and instant confirmations
Fewer messages of any kind
A different answer each time they ask
quiz.explanation: Customers receive faster responses, instant confirmations, quicker service, and more consistent communication. This improves satisfaction and builds trust.

quiz.question: What do employees do with the time that automation frees up, according to the productivity benefit?
options: Focus on innovation, customer relationships, growth and planning
Wait until the next repetitive task arrives
Check every automated message by hand
Copy the same data a second time
quiz.explanation: Instead of copying data or sending routine emails, employees can focus on higher-value work such as innovation, customer relationships, business growth and strategic planning.

quiz.question: Which phrase describes automation as a helper for increasing productivity?
options: A robot that replaces every worker
A manager that decides who gets paid
A digital assistant that handles repetitive work
A teacher that trains new staff
quiz.explanation: Automation becomes a digital assistant for repetitive work, so people can spend their time on work that needs creativity and judgment.

quiz.question: Which list names the areas where businesses use automation?
options: Education, healthcare, mining, farming and shipping
Education, healthcare, e-commerce, human resources and marketing
Healthcare, banking only, sports and fashion
Marketing, construction, e-commerce and tourism
quiz.explanation: Businesses use automation in education, healthcare, e-commerce, human resources and marketing, to reduce repetitive work, improve accuracy and provide faster service.

quiz.question: Which is the best example of the 'works 24 hours' benefit?
options: A staff member replies quickly by working an extra shift
A manager checks the system every hour overnight
A shop owner replies within minutes during the day
A booking confirmation goes out at 2 AM on a Sunday with nobody online
quiz.explanation: Automation can run at night, on weekends and on public holidays without a person, as long as the required systems are available.

quiz.question: At a supermarket, inventory reduces by one when bread is bought, with no manual stock update. What does this save?
options: The need to stock any bread at all
The need for customers to pay
The cost of the bread itself
The time staff would spend updating stock by hand
quiz.explanation: The system updates stock automatically, so nobody has to make manual stock updates. It is a simple example of saving time on repetitive work.

quiz.question: A website sends an instant 'Thank you' email to each person who submits a form. Which benefit does this show?
options: Saves money on staff pay
Reduces human errors in invoices
Improves customer experience
Increases the owner's own productivity
quiz.explanation: An instant confirmation is one of the things customers receive under better customer experience, and nobody has to type the message by hand.

quiz.question: A task takes 5 minutes and is repeated 30 times a day. How much time does it use daily?
options: 35 minutes
60 minutes
150 minutes
250 minutes
quiz.explanation: 5 x 30 = 150 minutes, which is 2 hours 30 minutes spent on repeating one task.

quiz.question: Chidi replies to the same 'Is this available?' messages dozens of times a day. What gain would automatic first replies give him?
options: He answers every message himself, but later in the evening
He stops replying to complaints and bulk orders for good
He saves hours daily and steps in only for messages needing his judgment
He saves time but can no longer reach customers directly
quiz.explanation: Chidi would save hours each day, respond faster even when busy in the shop, and personally handle only unusual messages such as bulk orders or complaints.

quiz.question: Task A takes 10 minutes and is done 50 times daily. Task B takes 2 minutes and is done 5 times daily. Which gives the bigger time saving when automated?
options: Task B, because it is quicker to do
Task A, because it uses 500 minutes a day against 10
Both save exactly the same time
Neither, because both are repetitive
quiz.explanation: Time saved depends on minutes per task multiplied by repeats. Task A uses 500 minutes a day and Task B uses only 10 minutes.

quiz.question: In the lesson summary, which results do businesses get from using automation in areas like education and healthcare?
options: Increase repetitive work, improve accuracy and provide faster service
Reduce repetitive work, improve accuracy and provide faster service
Reduce repetitive work, improve accuracy and provide slower service
Reduce repetitive work, improve guesswork and provide faster service
quiz.explanation: Businesses use automation in education, healthcare, e-commerce, human resources and marketing to reduce repetitive work, improve accuracy and provide faster service.

quiz.question: Which set of benefits matches what automation gives a business?
options: Saves time, reduces costs, minimizes human errors, increases productivity
Saves time, reduces costs, minimizes human errors, increases paperwork
Saves time, raises costs, minimizes human errors, increases productivity
Saves time, reduces costs, increases human errors, increases productivity
quiz.explanation: The lesson summary says automation saves time, reduces costs, minimizes human errors and increases productivity.

quiz.question: A task takes 8 minutes and is repeated 25 times a day. How many minutes does it use daily?
options: 33 minutes
120 minutes
200 minutes
320 minutes

scenario.situation: A training centre registers 200 applicants. For each one, staff check the form, send a WhatsApp message, send an email, update a spreadsheet and add the student to the class group. What is the main business value of automating these steps?

options.text: It saves time by handling the repeated steps for every applicant
options.outcome: Correct. The same steps repeat for each applicant, so automation frees staff time and keeps every applicant treated the same way.

options.text: It lets the system choose which applicants to accept
options.outcome: Wrong. Automation follows rules. It does not decide who gets accepted.

options.text: It removes the need to keep any applicant records
options.outcome: Wrong. Records are still needed. They are simply filled in without typing.

options.text: It makes each applicant wait for office hours
options.outcome: Wrong. Automation does the opposite, working whenever the required systems are available.

scenario.situation: A salon in Lagos gets booking messages on WhatsApp after closing time. Many customers book somewhere else because nobody replies until morning. Which benefit of automation fits this problem best?

options.text: Saves money by closing the salon earlier
options.outcome: Wrong. The problem is slow replies, not opening hours. Automation helps with the replies.

options.text: Works 24 hours, so replies go out at night and on weekends
options.outcome: Correct. Automation can run at any hour, including weekends and holidays, so customers are not left waiting.

options.text: Reduces errors by hiring more night staff
options.outcome: Wrong. Automation does not need extra night staff. It runs as long as the required systems are available.

options.text: Makes the stylists work faster
options.outcome: Wrong. Speed of styling is not what automation changes here.

scenario.situation: A school bursar types fee payments into a record all day. By evening she is tired and some amounts are entered wrongly. What is the main benefit of automating this?

options.text: It makes the bursar's tiredness disappear

options.text: It lets the system decide which parents should pay

options.text: It works only on public holidays

options.text: Automation never helps churches

options.text: Automation could handle the repeated entry, so more work gets done without adding staff

options.text: The admin team should stop recording members

objectives.text: Prepare to build a first workflow: look for repetitive tasks, write the process as simple steps, identify the trigger, identify the actions in order, keep the first automation simple; and sort the steps of a task into those software can do and those that need a human (the Manual vs Automated comparison chart).

quiz.question: What is the first step when preparing to build your first workflow?
options: Write the process as steps
Identify the trigger
Look for repetitive tasks
Open Zapier and start connecting apps
quiz.explanation: Step 1 is to look for repetitive tasks by asking, 'What do I do repeatedly?' Everything else comes after.

quiz.question: Which of these is a strong candidate for automation, according to Step 1 of the preparation?
options: Copying data from one place to another
Counselling a new church member in person
Settling an angry customer's complaint
Negotiating a partnership deal
quiz.explanation: Copying data is repetitive. The others need empathy, negotiation or a unique decision, so they need a human.

quiz.question: Why should you write the process down before building anything?
options: It makes the automation run faster
Automation tools will not open without it
It removes the need to test later
If you cannot explain a process clearly, you cannot automate it
quiz.explanation: Not understanding the process first is a beginner mistake. Writing each step makes the process clear enough to automate.

quiz.question: What does the material say about someone who can write out their process as steps?
options: They no longer need to identify a trigger
They are already thinking like an automation designer
They should automate everything at once
They must learn coding next
quiz.explanation: Being able to write the process means you are already thinking like an automation designer.

quiz.question: What question do you ask to identify the trigger?
options: What should happen next?
What starts this process?
How many steps are there?
Who will be notified?
quiz.explanation: Step 3 asks 'What starts this process?' The trigger is the event that starts the automation.

quiz.question: In a workflow for a customer completing registration, which one is the trigger?
options: Sending the welcome email
Notifying the sales team
Saving the customer details
The customer submits the registration form
quiz.explanation: The form submission is the event that starts everything. The email, notification and saving are actions that follow.

quiz.question: What question do you ask to identify the actions?
options: What should happen next?
What starts this process?
Who is my competitor?
How much will this cost?
quiz.explanation: Step 4 asks 'What should happen next?' and then you list each action in order.

quiz.question: What size should your first automation be?
options: Ten triggers and many actions
As large as the whole business process
One trigger and one or two actions
It does not matter at all
quiz.explanation: Step 5 says a simple workflow with one trigger and one or two actions is enough to build confidence.

quiz.question: Why should your first automation be kept simple?
options: Simple workflows never need any testing at all
Software tools refuse to run longer workflows
Small wins build confidence before bigger tasks
A short workflow always saves more money
quiz.explanation: Start small, learn, and improve gradually. A simple workflow with one trigger and one or two actions is enough to build confidence.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the Manual vs Automated comparison chart?
options: To sort a task's steps into those software can do and those needing a human
To count how many hours each task takes in a week
To choose which automation app to download first
To list the people responsible for each step of a task
quiz.explanation: The chart breaks a real task into steps and shows which are repetitive (automatable) and which genuinely need a human.

quiz.question: How are the two columns of the chart labelled?
options: Automated on the left, Manual on the right
Manual on the left, Automated on the right
Easy on the left, Hard on the right
Trigger on the left, Action on the right
quiz.explanation: Step 2 says to label the left column Manual and the right column Automated.

quiz.question: How many steps should your Manual column have at least?
options: One
Two
Four or five
Twenty
quiz.explanation: The expected result of Step 3 is at least four or five separate steps written down.

quiz.question: Which question do you ask about each step to decide whether to tick it?
options: If this happened the same way 100 times, would anything change?
If this step cost 100 naira, would the owner care?
If 100 customers saw this step, would they like it?
If this step were skipped 100 times, would anyone notice?
quiz.explanation: Step 4 uses the 100-times test. If nothing would change, you tick the step as a strong automation candidate.

quiz.question: What does a tick on a step mean?
options: The step is unimportant
The step must be deleted
The step needs a human
The step is repetitive and predictable
quiz.explanation: A tick means repetitive and predictable, not unimportant.

quiz.question: Which wording style is recommended for the Automated column?
options: Personal wording like 'I remember to send the message...'
Passive wording like 'A message may go out someday...'
Active, software wording like 'Message is sent automatically...'
Formal wording like 'The customer is kindly requested...'
quiz.explanation: The Pro Tip suggests active, software-focused language such as 'Software detects...', 'System logs...', 'Message is sent automatically...'.

quiz.question: Step 3 says not to skip any small action when listing the Manual steps. Why?
options: Small actions are always the ones to automate
The more detail you capture, the easier the next steps are
The chart is marked by how many steps it holds
Skipped steps get ticked automatically later
quiz.explanation: Capturing every small action makes it easier to tick, rewrite and circle steps in the later parts of the chart.

quiz.question: In Illustration 1, which steps do you cross out under Automated?
options: Every step the owner dislikes doing
Every step that takes more than five minutes
Every step that involves a customer
Every step a computer could do without a human
quiz.explanation: You cross out every step a computer could do without a human, then circle what is left for the person.

quiz.question: What shift does the light switch versus motion-sensor example show?
options: From a person noticing and acting to software noticing and acting
From a slow light to a bright light
From software noticing and acting to a person noticing and acting
From a small room to a bigger room
quiz.explanation: A switch needs a person to notice and act. A motion sensor notices and switches on by itself, which is the shift automation makes.

quiz.question: Which description fits a great automation candidate?
options: It happens often, follows the same steps, and a short delay is harmless
It happens rarely, changes each time, and must be done to the second
It needs empathy, follows no pattern, and happens often
It needs negotiation, is unique, and is done once a year
quiz.explanation: A great candidate is frequent, follows the same steps every time, and can be slightly delayed without disaster.

quiz.question: Which is a beginner mistake mentioned for preparing a first workflow?
options: Starting with one small task
Testing the automation several times
Trying to automate everything
Protecting passwords
quiz.explanation: Mistake 1 is trying to automate everything. Not every task needs automation, so start with simple, repetitive ones.

scenario.situation: Ngozi runs a hair salon in Enugu. She answers 'What time do you open?' on WhatsApp about forty times a week, always with the same reply. She wants to start automating but has never built a workflow.

options.text: Start with the task she finds most complicated
options.outcome: Complicated tasks are poor first picks. Strong first picks are simple and repetitive.

options.text: Start with the repeated reply about opening time
options.outcome: It is repetitive and predictable, so it fits Step 1 well.

options.text: Start with advising clients on which hairstyle suits them
options.outcome: That advice needs her personal judgment each time, so it is a weak candidate.

options.text: Try to automate all her WhatsApp messages at once
options.outcome: Trying to automate everything is a beginner mistake.

scenario.situation: Emeka wants to automate how his bakery handles online orders. He opens an automation tool at once but cannot say what the steps of taking an order are.

options.text: Keep clicking until something works
options.outcome: Without a clear process he may build the wrong thing and never know why.

options.text: Stop and write the order process as simple steps first
options.outcome: If you cannot explain the process, you cannot automate it. Writing the steps comes before building.

options.text: Copy another bakery's workflow exactly
options.outcome: Another business has different steps, so it may not fit his orders.

scenario.situation: A school bursar lists the process: parent pays fees, receipt sent, record updated in a sheet. She is asked what the trigger is.

options.text: Sending the receipt
options.outcome: The receipt is an action performed after the trigger occurs.

options.text: Updating the sheet
options.outcome: This is an action, not the event that starts the process.

options.text: The parent paying the fees
options.outcome: Payment is the event that starts the process. The rest are actions that follow.

scenario.situation: Tunde, a shop owner, is listing a workflow. He writes: 'send thank-you message, then save the order, then the customer pays'. A friend says something is off.

options.text: Nothing is wrong because order never matters
options.outcome: The workflow runs one step after another, so order does matter.

options.text: Put the payment first as the trigger, then the actions in order
options.outcome: The trigger starts the process, and Step 4 says to list each action in order after it.

options.text: Delete the payment from the list
options.outcome: The payment is a likely trigger, so removing it leaves nothing to start the workflow.

scenario.situation: Aisha, an NYSC member, wants her first automation to do twelve things when a Google Form is submitted, including emails, folders and reports.

options.text: Build all twelve at once to save time
options.outcome: Very large workflows too soon often become confusing and hard to fix.

options.text: Abandon the idea completely
options.outcome: Automation is still useful. She only needs to start smaller.

options.text: Reduce it to one trigger and one or two actions first
options.outcome: A simple workflow is enough to build confidence, and she can improve gradually.

scenario.situation: Bisi lists her tasks at a boutique. Which one should she pick as the best first automation target?

options.text: Comforting a customer who received the wrong dress
options.outcome: This needs empathy, so it needs a human.

options.text: Deciding a special price for a regular customer
options.outcome: This is a unique decision for each customer.

options.text: Sending the same 'Your order is ready' message to every customer
options.outcome: It is frequent, follows the same steps and a small delay is harmless.

options.text: Negotiating with a fabric supplier
options.outcome: Negotiation needs a human every time.

scenario.situation: Kunle drew a Manual vs Automated chart for replying to enquiries. He ticked 'Decide whether to offer a discount'. His instructor asks him to look again.

options.text: Keep it ticked because discounts happen often

options.text: Un-tick it, because a step involving deciding needs a human
options.outcome: Steps involving deciding, negotiating or comforting must be un-ticked and circled.

options.text: Choose a different task straight away
options.outcome: Changing tasks does not solve it. Adding detail does.

options.text: Tick that one step and finish
options.outcome: One vague step gives no way to see which parts need a human.

options.text: Rewrite them under Automated

options.text: Frequent is not the same as automatable, so it still needs a human
options.outcome: A step can happen often and still need a human touch because it needs judgment.

options.text: Frequent steps are always safe to automate
options.outcome: Frequency alone is not the test. Judgment steps still need a person.

options.outcome: A fixed reply that never changes does not need one.

options.text: Strong, because the same reply is sent every time
options.outcome: The message is repetitive and predictable with no judgment needed.

options.text: Detecting the money
options.outcome: This is the same every time, so it can be ticked.

options.text: Sending the SMS
options.outcome: The same message sent each time is a strong automation step.

options.text: List each action that should happen next, in order
options.outcome: After the trigger is found, Step 4 asks 'What should happen next?' and lists each action in order.

options.text: Leave it blank until later
options.outcome: Each step should be decided with the 100-times question.

options.outcome: A step that never changes is repetitive and predictable, so it gets a tick.

options.text: Circle it as human-only
options.outcome: Nothing would change over 100 repeats, so it should not be circled.

scenario.situation: Ibrahim made a chart for his shop task and ticked nothing. Every step is circled as needing a human. He thinks nothing in his task can be automated.

options.text: Tick every step so the chart looks balanced
options.outcome: Ticking judgment steps is a common mistake. Only steps that never change get a tick.

options.text: Circle the steps again to be sure
options.outcome: Circling again changes nothing. The steps must be checked against the 100-times question.

options.text: Ask the 100-times question again for each step before deciding
options.outcome: If a step would not change over 100 repeats it deserves a tick. Re-checking may find steps that are repetitive.

scenario.situation: Yusuf tries an automation for the first time and asks which of these is the right first question to ask about his work.

options.text: What is the biggest expense?
options.outcome: Cost is not the starting question for finding a task.

options.text: What do I do repeatedly?
options.outcome: Step 1 starts with finding repeated tasks.

options.text: Which tool is the newest?
options.outcome: The preparation is about mindset, not tools.

scenario.situation: Grace has a plan: customer places an order, then she lists actions as 'Send confirmation, Create record, Notify the packer'. Her friend asks what each of those is called.

options.text: Actions, which are tasks performed after the trigger
options.outcome: Actions do the work once the trigger starts the automation.

options.text: A workflow, because there are three
options.outcome: A workflow is the whole sequence of triggers and actions.

options.text: Triggers, because they come first
options.outcome: The trigger is the order. These come afterward.

scenario.situation: Mr Bako, a school bursar, thinks a workflow must be either 100% manual or 100% automated. He wants to automate fee receipts but still decide payment plans for struggling parents himself, so he is unsure what to do.

options.text: Automate the fee receipts and keep payment plan decisions with himself
options.outcome: Most good automations are a mix. Repetitive parts run by themselves while a human makes judgment calls.

options.text: Automate the payment plan decisions as well, so everything is automatic
options.outcome: Decisions about struggling parents need judgment, so they should stay with a person.

options.text: Keep both tasks fully manual so the workflow stays pure
options.outcome: Receipts are repetitive and predictable, so doing them by hand wastes his time.

options.text: Automate nothing until every task can be automated
options.outcome: A workflow does not need to be fully automated to be useful. Repetitive steps can start now.
